news.Title: HSBC Just Turned Bullish on Cisco Stock Again. Here’s Why It Expects 40% Upside.
news.Content:
Cisco Systems (CSCO) has long worn the label of a mature networking giant, rarely linked to rapid growth. Yet now, the company is shaking up Wall Street's expectations. Fueled by a wave of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investment, strong enterprise demand, and an exceptional quarter, Cisco has prompted HSBC to abandon its cautious stance, upgrade the stock to "Buy," and raise its price target to $133.

With the bank forecasting nearly 40% upside, Cisco's growth revival is quickly becoming impossible to ignore. Let's take a closer look.

HSBC's Change of Heart Has a Clear Catalyst

On Nov. 17, HSBC raised CSCO stock to "Buy" from "Hold" and increased its price target to $133 from $120. The new target implies approximately 40% potential upside from current levels. The move is notable because HSBC had downgraded Cisco stock from "Buy" to "Hold" in August, cutting its target from $137 to $120. Its latest upgrade reverses that decision, driven by a stronger networking outlook, firmer AI-related demand, and a valuation it considers attractive relative to growth.

HSBC expects Cisco's networking revenue to compound at 19.2% annually from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2029. The firm also forecasts adjusted EPS to grow 14.9% annually from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2031. The $133 price target applies a 23 times multiple to the estimated next-12-month adjusted EPS of $5.78. In other words, the valuation depends on earnings growth continuing and investors maintaining that earnings multiple.

The Quarter Was Strong Because Demand Reached Beyond AI

Cisco's first quarter of fiscal 2027 performance encouraged HSBC to shift from caution to a more optimistic stance. The company reported $18.5 billion in revenue, up 24% year-over-year (YOY). Adjusted EPS rose 40% YOY to $1.40, while adjusted operating margin reached 37.8%. CFO Mark Patterson said the company exceeded the high end of its guidance for revenue, operating margin, and EPS. Cisco focused not just on shipping more equipment but on turning the stronger quarter into higher profitability.

Story Continues

Product revenue rose 32% YOY to $14.7 billion, while services revenue grew just 1% to $3.9 billion. Networking stole the spotlight with a remarkable 43% increase, while security, collaboration, and software each posted steady gains of 7%, 8%, and 8%, respectively, with software reaching $6.1 billion. Clearly, hardware drove this acceleration, not services.

Orders provide an important check on revenue momentum. Product orders climbed 21%, backed by double-digit growth across every region. Service provider and cloud orders soared 47%, while enterprise and public-sector orders advanced 15% and 13%. Networking orders surged 28%, marking its ninth-straight quarter of double-digit gains. This broad-based recovery reduces reliance on hyperscalers.

The order picture also extends into traditional networking. Campus networking orders increased 14%, and telecom orders rose 20%. Cisco is benefiting not only from new AI data centers but also from customers upgrading enterprise networks and connectivity. These projects can broaden the addressable demand pool and make the growth profile less dependent on the timing of a few large AI deployments.

Nonetheless, hyperscalers still remain the biggest growth catalyst. Cisco projects $9 billion in AI infrastructure sales to these customers in fiscal 2027, up from about $4 billion in fiscal 2026 and higher than its earlier $7.5 billion forecast. Management pointed to stronger orders, better visibility, and three AI design wins with Silicon One systems and 1.6-terabit optics.

Cisco ended the quarter with $46.2 billion in remaining performance obligations (RPO), up 8% YOY, and annual recurring revenue (ARR) of $32.7 billion, up 4%. Subscription revenue accounted for 44% of sales. No doubt, there is a sharp gap between hardware and services growth, but these numbers also reflect a steadier revenue foundation as networking equipment demand moves through its cycle.

Upbeat Outlook Adds to the Bullish Case

Cisco raised its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $74.8 billion to $75.8 billion and adjusted EPS to $5.47 to $5.53. The revenue midpoint implies roughly 19% YOY growth. For Q2, management expects revenue of $18 billion to $18.2 billion and EPS of $1.34 to $1.36.

Yet the quarter revealed a price to pay. Adjusted gross margin edged down to 65.6%, and product gross margin slipped to 63.7%. Management pointed to a heavier hardware mix and rising memory costs, with some relief from productivity gains and pricing. The very products fueling growth are, for now, less profitable than those they are replacing. Management remains confident it will reach a 36% adjusted operating margin for fiscal 2027, up from 34.8% in fiscal 2026, suggesting productivity and scale gains could help offset mounting pressures.

Operating cash flow surged 36% to $4.4 billion, highlighting strong financial momentum. Now, all eyes are on whether rising memory and component costs will persist as hardware claims a bigger slice of sales. Cisco returned $3.7 billion to shareholders during the quarter through dividends and share buybacks, showing its capacity to generate strong cash flow while fueling growth and rewarding investors.

The $9 Billion AI Opportunity Is Not Free of Its Costs

Cisco's AI forecast depends on customers deploying systems on schedule. Management flagged optics supply as a potential constraint, while the second half of the year will test the company with tougher benchmarks. Delayed hyperscaler projects could shift revenue between quarters, and lower gross margins may limit how much sales growth reaches earnings. These risks lurk behind that bullish forecast.

Basically, HSBC is betting networking growth isn't a one-quarter spike. Its 19.2% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) forecast and $133 price target rest on the belief that AI infrastructure and broader networking demand will keep powering ahead. While some analysts have cut their price targets, they have also acknowledged the strong results and retained bullish ratings.

Cisco Must Prove It Can Keep Growth on Track

Cisco's story extends far beyond the $9 billion AI forecast. Surging networking revenue, strong orders from diverse customers, and rising guidance fuel its growth engine. The challenge is turning this demand into profitable sales while managing component costs and supply constraints. The next quarters will reveal whether Cisco can turn orders into deliveries, stabilize margins, and meet its ambitious EPS targets. If the company delivers, CSCO stock can hit HSBC's bullish target of $133 or even the Street's high price estimate of $150.

Overall, Cisco stock holds a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating on Wall Street. Of the 26 analysts covering the stock, 16 have a "Strong Buy," one has a "Moderate Buy," and nine have a "Hold" rating. The average price target sits at $129.65, suggesting a possible 37% climb, while the most bullish estimate of $150 implies potential upside of 58% from current levels.

Investing.com — The AI chip trade has unraveled this month. Intel's weak forecast set off a broad semiconductor sell-off, and Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) had already slid about 22% between the first reports of its $115 billion bid for Lumentum and the deal's announcement. Even Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE)—the laser maker supplying the optical links inside AI data centers—has plunged 34.0% over the past month to $551.07, including an 11.8% slide in the past week alone.

The headline growth is what makes Lumentum tempting, but the stock no longer trades on its own results. Analysts forecast 121.5% revenue growth and 130.6% EPS growth, yet Marvell's all-stock agreement pays Lumentum shareholders a fixed 4.5 Marvell shares for each share they own, so every slide in Marvell now lands directly on Lumentum's price. GAAP earnings also remain negative at -7.6 times trailing earnings, and InvestingPro's valuation models rate the stock merely "Fair" at $566.14, just 2.7% above the share price. That leaves dip-buyers taking on Marvell's swings without a valuation cushion of their own.

The Laser Supplier AI Cannot Get Enough Of

Lumentum makes its money selling the lasers and optical components that carry data between AI servers, and it sells them into a market where demand has outrun supply. It holds dominant share in indium phosphide lasers and high-speed EMLs, commands 70% to 80% of the pump laser market, and is the only merchant supplier of optical circuit switches with a proven shipping track record. Pump laser shipments surged more than 80% year-over-year, backed by three-year take-or-pay agreements with major hyperscalers.

Fiscal fourth-quarter results showed how much that position now earns. Revenue surged 109% year-over-year and 23% sequentially to $1.01 billion, the eighth straight quarter of growth, while non-GAAP gross margin topped 50% for the first time and non-GAAP operating margin expanded 2,160 basis points to 36.6%. The first quarter of fiscal 2027 then beat estimates, with revenue climbing 136.5% year-over-year to $1.26 billion and EPS of $4.57.

Story Continues

The negative trailing multiple stems from a single accounting charge rather than weak operations. A one-time, non-cash $7.8 billion charge from converting convertible debt into equity produced a fourth-quarter GAAP net loss of $7.2 billion, yet first-quarter GAAP net income reached $360.3 million.

Wall Street Cools, Fair Value Holds the Line

Wall Street has turned more cautious since the deal. B. Riley cut Lumentum to Neutral with a $770 target, Stifel moved to Hold at $806, and UBS holds at $686, while Bernstein SocGen still rates it a Buy at $700. Every one of those targets sits above the current share price, and the average analyst target of roughly $1,070 sits far higher. Estimates keep climbing: 16 analysts have revised EPS forecasts higher over the past 90 days with none lower, and consensus calls for $28.41 in fiscal 2027 and $45.84 in fiscal 2028.

InvestingPro's Fair Value models see far less room to run, placing intrinsic value at $566.14 per share—just 2.7% above the share price and well below the Street's average target.

The main risk is that Lumentum's fate is no longer its own. Marvell's slide has already reduced the implied deal value from the roughly $1,132 per share it carried at announcement, and closing is not expected until the first half of 2028, subject to stockholder and regulatory approvals that could include China. Investor-rights firms have launched investigations into whether the ratio fairly values Lumentum shareholders, and insiders sold about $86 million of stock in the three months before the announcement.

A Growth Story on Someone Else's Clock

Lumentum has shown it can turn the AI buildout into record revenue and expanding margins. Until the Marvell deal closes or breaks, though, its share price will track Marvell's stock and the regulatory calendar more closely than its own order book.

news.Title: Can MRVL's Custom Silicon Business Drive Its Next Growth Phase?
news.Content:
Marvell Technology MRVL is expanding its presence in the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure market through its custom silicon business. The company develops custom compute and connectivity solutions for hyperscalers seeking to build and optimize AI infrastructure. Its portfolio includes custom XPUs and XPU-attach products, which help address growing requirements for AI computing, memory and data movement.

MRVL's custom silicon opportunity is gaining traction as hyperscalers expand their investments in AI infrastructure. The company expects demand for its XPU and XPU-attach solutions to accelerate in the second half of fiscal 2027. Management remains confident that custom silicon revenues will more than double year over year in fiscal 2028, with further acceleration expected in fiscal 2029. This provides greater visibility into the business' contribution to MRVL's multi-year growth outlook.

An expanded commercial agreement with a Tier 1 hyperscaler further strengthens this opportunity. The agreement covers existing programs, new design wins and potential future projects. Its scope extends beyond AI inference accelerators to include storage controllers, network interface controllers (NICs), memory interface controllers and near-memory compute solutions associated with the customer's tensor processing unit ecosystem. The broader engagement creates opportunities for MRVL to supply multiple components across AI computing and connectivity architectures.

The company is also benefiting from its expanding relationships across the AI ecosystem. Its strategic partnership with NVIDIA and investments in networking technologies complement its custom silicon portfolio. By combining custom compute solutions with high-speed connectivity, switching and optical interconnect technologies, MRVL is positioning itself to address multiple requirements of increasingly complex AI infrastructure. This broader portfolio could strengthen its competitive position as hyperscalers develop next-generation AI systems.

However, the expansion carries execution and profitability risks. Custom silicon programs typically depend on customer design decisions, deployment schedules and production ramps. Moreover, management expects the accelerating custom product mix to weigh on near-term gross margins. MRVL's increasing dependence on large hyperscalers also raises customer concentration risks. Nevertheless, sustained design wins and the expected revenue acceleration position custom silicon as an important driver of its growth through fiscal 2028 and beyond.

How Competitors Fare Against MRVL

MRVL faces stiff competition from Broadcom AVGO and Advanced Micro Devices AMD. Broadcom is a leader in the domain of custom silicon solutions for data centers. Broadcom's advanced 3.5D XDSiP packaging platform is critical to ensure the performance and efficiency of custom AI XPUs.

Broadcom's relationships with leading hyperscale and frontier AI customers give it direct insight into workload requirements and help shape differentiated accelerators. The company continues to work with six core XPU customers across multiyear programs. Advanced Micro Devices is another established player in the custom silicon solutions and AI accelerator market. Advanced Micro Devices offers semi-custom SoCs and Instinct Accelerators to power data centers. AMD is broadening its data center AI opportunity from Instinct accelerators to the Helios rack-scale platform.

news.Title: Analysts Turned Bullish on These 5 Stocks on Tuesday
news.Content:
Wall Street is trading on what the Federal Reserve does next, even as analysts keep changing their ratings. The Fed held its key rate steady at its October 27 to 28 meeting, after raising it in September for the first time in three years.

Minutes released on November 18 showed that nearly all officials expect a quarter-point increase in December, and two raised the idea of a half-point move. Wall Street puts the odds of a December hike near 95%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

The jump in expectations began on November 10, when a hotter-than-expected October inflation report sent the 2-year Treasury yield up more than 18 basis points, its biggest one-day rise since April 2025, Reuters reported.

Why the Fed May Not Be Done Raising Rates

Fed Governor Christopher Waller backs the larger move. He said inflation is "headed in the wrong direction and it's spreading out," and he put core inflation at about a 3.5% annual rate over the past three months, against the Fed's 2% target. Readers following analysts' favorite growth names can find more in our ranking of aggressive growth picks from Wall Street analysts .

New York Fed President John Williams disagrees and does not think the situation calls for dramatic action. STMicroelectronics Could Reach New Highs—Here's What Needs to Happen

STMicroelectronics (NYSE:STM) expects data center revenue to more than double in 2027, with silicon photonics leading the increase as demand for AI infrastructure reshapes the chipmaker's business, President and CEO Jean-Marc Chery said at an event in Barcelona.

news.Title: Jim Cramer’s AI Hyperscale List: 5 Core Infrastructure Stocks for 2027
news.Content:
When a cloud company orders thousands of AI servers, the date it can put them to work often depends on when the local utility can deliver power. Contractors prepare the site and build the grid connection. Inside the facility, electrical equipment distributes power to the server racks, cooling systems carry heat away from the chips, and switches and fiber links allow processors across those racks to train a model together.

At the end of June 2026, CBRE tracked 7.48 gigawatts of wholesale data-center capacity under construction across eight major U.S. markets, with 80.4% already leased. For those projects, securing power on schedule can matter more than finding tenants. On October 28, California's grid operator approved a proposal that would let large customers connect before all transmission upgrades are complete if they can reduce their electricity use when the grid requires it.

For investors, the debate over how much power a data center can draw reaches beyond the utility. In August, CNBC's Mad Money host Jim Cramer explained why local opposition to new projects made him take a closer look at the order book of a company his Charitable Trust owned.

In November, a cloud operator raised its revenue forecast, lifting shares across the AI supply chain. A leading AI chipmaker ranked 10th in our ranking of the infrastructure stocks with the most upside implied by analysts' price targets following that report. However, the AI buildout extends well beyond chips, creating opportunities across the infrastructure needed to power, cool, and connect hyperscale data centers.

Methodology

We reviewed his public comments from March through November 2026 and selected 5 stocks of companies that build, power, cool, or connect hyperscale AI facilities. We ranked the stocks in ascending order of market capitalization.

Market Capitalization: ~$104 billion

Through its xScale joint ventures, it develops and operates facilities where hyperscale customers lease capacity, measured in megawatts, to house and power their servers. When another caller asked about Equinix on May 20, Cramer took a different view of the company's place in the data-center buildout .

news.Title: STMicroelectronics Targets Double STM32 Revenue by 2028 as AI Demand Grows
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in STMicroelectronics N.V.? Here are five stocks we like better.

STMicroelectronics aims to double STM32 revenue from 2025 to 2028 , with market share already back to about 23% and potentially reaching 25%–30% by 2028.

AI data centers are a major growth driver: ST expects microcontrollers to account for more than 30% of its data-center revenue in 2026 and data-center microcontroller revenue to double in 2027. Industrial automation, cooling and power delivery are also expected to support growth.

Further opportunities include automotive-grade STM32A chips, with revenue expected to start in 2028, and humanoid robotics, where a typical robot may use 100 or more microcontrollers. ST is also expanding its China supply strategy and adapting its software tools for AI coding agents.

STMicroelectronics Could Reach New Highs—Here's What Needs to Happen

STMicroelectronics (NYSE:STM) aims to double revenue from its STM32 microcontroller business between 2025 and 2028, betting that demand from artificial intelligence infrastructure, industrial systems, robotics and automotive applications will expand its market.

Remi El-Ouazzane, president of the company's Microcontrollers, Digital ICs and RF Products Group, said during a conference call that STM32's market-share recovery was running about 12 months ahead of schedule. He said the business had returned to its nominal share of about 23% and could reach between 25% and 30% by 2028, with the result more likely to be toward the upper end of that range if the revenue goal is met.

Apple, Meta, and SpaceX Are Driving a Device Boom—These 3 Stocks Could Benefit

El-Ouazzane said third-quarter 2026 revenue was 25% below its second-quarter 2023 peak, but the conditions behind those figures differed. The earlier peak benefited from inventory accumulation and price increases, he said, while distribution inventory is now below standard targets and the book-to-bill ratio has remained above one for four quarters.

Data centers and industrial markets

ST expects microcontrollers to account for more than 30% of its data-center-related revenue in 2026 and expects its data-center microcontroller revenue to double in 2027, El-Ouazzane said. The chips are used in optical connectivity, compute boards and power conversion systems.

Industrial Chips Are in Rally Mode—5 Ways to Play

He said data centers would contribute a significant portion of STM32's growth but would not account for all of it. Industrial automation, cooling and power delivery are also growing, he said. The company expects a healthy industrial market through at least 2027 following an inventory correction during the prior three years.

Story Continues

ST has a strong position in microcontrollers used in optical transceivers, El-Ouazzane said, attributing it to the company's developer ecosystem and broad product portfolio. He said ST's planning assumes some loss of optical market share, given its current position.

Automotive and robotics opportunities

→ NVIDIA's Turbulence Could Have Ripple Effects Across Quantum Computing

ST is extending its STM32 platform into automotive-grade and higher-safety applications with the STM32A family. El-Ouazzane said revenue from the automotive products should begin in 2028, remain modest initially and become more meaningful in 2029.

Volkswagen has adopted STM32A, he said, citing the automaker as an example of demand for a unified platform and software ecosystem. El-Ouazzane added that ST's previously stated automotive microcontroller ambition remained valid, though it would take slightly longer than initially expected because of subdued market conditions.

In humanoid robotics, El-Ouazzane said a typical robot contains about 100 or more microcontrollers. He estimated that microcontrollers represent approximately 20% of the $800 in components per robot that ST could address. The company is working with leading industry participants, he said.

China, pricing and software

El-Ouazzane said ST is gaining STM32 market share in China through a strategy that offers the same product through two supply chains. The company delivered its first fully made-in-China STM32 products in the first quarter of 2026 and is extending the approach to additional product families.

He said the Chinese business was not dilutive to the group's gross margin, citing its product mix, and that market-share gains had not been driven by pricing. More broadly, ST intends to pass through cost increases without exploiting inflation, he said, adding that the company had potentially been overly aggressive with price increases in 2022 and 2023.

ST's STM32Cube software ecosystem is approaching 2 million active developers, El-Ouazzane said. The company is adapting its tools for AI coding agents and offers an AI-powered technical support assistant. It is also exploring possible bolt-on acquisitions that could strengthen its software ecosystem or its position in physical AI and humanoid robotics, he said.

About STMicroelectronics (NYSE:STM)

STMicroelectronics is a global semiconductor company that designs, develops and manufactures chips and related products for customers in a range of industries. Its portfolio includes microcontrollers, analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits, power semiconductors, sensors, and microelectromechanical systems (MEMS). The company's products are used in automotive systems, industrial equipment, communications devices, computers and consumer electronics. Its offerings support applications such as vehicle control and safety, factory automation, power management, and motion and environmental sensing.

news.Title: NVIDIA vs. Cisco: One AI Stock Looks Like a Better Buy Now
news.Content:
Despite NVIDIA Corporation 's NVDA strong quarterly performance, leadership uncertainty and rising artificial intelligence (AI) spending concerns could pose a challenge in the future. However, Cisco Systems, Inc .'s CSCO stable management and diversified business portfolio could position it as a better stock to buy now. Let's explore –

NVIDIA Sees Record Growth, Issues Strong Q4 Revenue Guidance

NVIDIA delivered another strong quarter, with revenues surging 103% year over year to $115.8 billion in the fiscal third quarter of 2027, according to the company's Nov. 17 press release. It also posted a 20% sequential rise from $96.2 billion in the previous quarter. NVIDIA's triple-digit growth rate highlighted that strong AI spending benefited the company, with tech companies investing significantly in computing capacity.

The Data Center business remains its primary growth driver, with revenues jumping 110% year over year and 21% sequentially to $107.6 billion. This result shows NVIDIA is making the most of hyperscalers' massive investments in AI-driven data centers. By the way, NVIDIA is converting its impressive revenue growth into noteworthy profits as well. Its GAAP net income jumped 105% year over year to $65.3 billion.

Looking ahead, NVIDIA expects revenues of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, in the fiscal fourth quarter of 2027, which would represent a 12% sequential rise. That's a strong revenue growth projection, especially since it doesn't include China-related Data Center compute revenues. NVIDIA also expects its earnings outlook to remain strong in the fiscal fourth quarter.

NVIDIA Is Dominating AI, But Is Cisco the Better Investment?

NVIDIA's strong fiscal third-quarter performance and optimistic fiscal fourth-quarter outlook suggest the company is not only benefiting from the AI boom but also converting that growth into solid revenues and earnings growth. However, the latest controversy surrounding NVIDIA's boardroom drama and the subsequent ouster of Jensen Huang as CEO is a significant concern for investors in the future.

NVIDIA will lose a visionary leader, whose continuous innovation helped the company maintain a competitive position in the rapidly evolving AI market. His earlier investments in graphics processing units helped NVIDIA establish a competitive advantage against its peers. He also played a crucial role in building partnerships among major tech players, and his departure could give an undue advantage to rivals such as Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. AMD.

Story Continues

Moving ahead, NVIDIA's capability to sustain an extraordinary growth rate without Huang at the helm will be closely monitored, and any leadership uncertainty could dent investors' confidence. But as NVIDIA grapples with leadership succession, Cisco stands out for its stable succession planning and management continuity. The company's CEO, Chuck Robbins, has held the position since 2015 and has assured investors that in his absence, the company's strategic decisions and execution won't be hampered.

Growing concerns about the sustainability of AI spending could create additional uncertainty around NVIDIA's future growth trajectory. Cisco, on the other hand, has a diversified revenue stream, making it less dependent on the AI boom. It can benefit from broader IT spending, providing additional growth opportunities, and could offer greater resilience if AI-related spending moderates.

Cisco reported record revenues of $18.5 billion in the fiscal first quarter of 2027, up 24% year over year, according to the company's Nov. 12 press release. However, Cisco's revenue growth wasn't only dependent on AI investments by hyperscalers; it was broad-based, across various business segments like networking, cybersecurity, collaboration and software.

Additionally, similar to NVIDIA, Cisco is translating its revenue growth into stronger earnings and demonstrating operational efficiency. Its GAAP net income jumped 59% year over year to $4.6 billion in the fiscal first quarter. Furthermore, management has raised its full-year 2027 revenue guidance to $74.8-$75.8 billion and increased its earnings expectations, reflecting confidence in future business growth.

Therefore, while NVIDIA offers greater AI-driven growth potential, Cisco's management stability, diversified revenue streams, and positive outlook make it an attractive investment for investors looking for more balanced growth. news.Content:
Cisco Systems CSCO shares have dropped 6.7% in the past three trading sessions after the company reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Nov. 12. Shares fell 6.2% in the Nov. 13 trading session, despite CSCO reporting record revenues and earnings and raising its fiscal 2027 guidance. The primary concerns were declining gross margins, higher component costs, slowing product-order growth and uncertainty surrounding the sustainability of AI-driven demand. However, does the dip offer an opportunity to take a position in CSCO shares? Let's find out.

Cisco Suffers From Margin Pressure, Moderating Order Growth

Investor concerns around margin pressure and the quality of forward growth despite very strong top-line results have been plaguing Cisco shares. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, non-GAAP gross margin contracted 250 basis points (bps) year over year to 65.6%, while non-GAAP product gross margin declined 350 bps to 63.7%. The contraction primarily reflected a higher mix of hardware revenues, particularly AI networking infrastructure and elevated memory costs. Cisco's growing exposure to relatively lower-margin hardware raised concerns regarding its ability to sustain profitability as AI infrastructure revenues accelerate.

Cisco increased its fiscal 2027 hyperscaler AI infrastructure revenue forecast to $9 billion from $7.5 billion. However, the rapid expansion of this hardware-intensive business is expected to weigh on product margins. Moreover, moderating product order growth is a concern. Although total product orders increased 21% year over year in the reported quarter, growth slowed from 35% in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. This raised concerns that Cisco's near-term demand momentum might be moderating following a period of significant expansion. The company faces tougher year-over-year comparisons, particularly in campus networking, and is also expected to suffer from uneven spending patterns of hyperscale customers.

Cisco now expects second-quarter fiscal 2027 revenues between $18 billion and $18.2 billion, implying a sequential decline from the reported $18.52 billion. Non-GAAP earnings per share are expected between $1.34 and $1.36, below the fiscal first quarter's reported figure of $1.40 per share. Although the company raised its fiscal 2027 outlook, the sequential moderation in revenue and earnings raised concerns regarding the near-term growth trajectory.

Year to date (YTD), Cisco shares have returned 23.5%, outperforming the broader Zacks Computer & Technology sector's appreciation of 3.5%. Cisco has underperformed peers, including Hewlett Packard Enterprise HPE and Arista Networks ANET, but outperformed Broadcom AVGO over the same time frame. news.Title: Applied Materials vs. Marvell Technology: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
news.Content:
As the race for dominance in artificial intelligence intensifies, choosing the right infrastructure provider is critical. Should you invest in equipment giant Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) or connectivity specialist Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL)?

Applied Materials supplies the tools that actually build the chips, making it a foundational player in the semiconductor ecosystem. Marvell designs the custom chips and networking components that move data between servers. Comparing these two reveals different ways to play the ongoing shift toward high-performance computing and massive data center expansion.

The case for Applied Materials

Applied Materials sells materials engineering solutions used to produce nearly every new chip and advanced display in the world. It serves a concentrated customer base of logic, foundry, and memory manufacturers, including giants like Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) and Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU). Two specific customers accounted for approximately 19% and 15% of net revenue, respectively. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 25, 2026, revenue reached nearly $34.4 billion. This represented growth of roughly 21.4% compared to the prior period, driven by strong demand for advanced chipmaking equipment. Net income totaled approximately $10.1 billion, showcasing the profitability possible at this scale.

As of Applied Materials' October 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3. This ratio measures total debt against shareholder equity, with lower numbers typically suggesting less financial leverage. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, is roughly 2.3. For those following semiconductor stocks , strong cash flow is vital for R&D. In the fiscal year ended Oct. 25, 2026, free cash flow was nearly $6.2 billion.

The case for Marvell Technology

Marvell Technology operates as a fabless supplier, meaning it designs high-end semiconductor solutions but outsources the actual manufacturing. The company focuses on data center core networks and the network edge, serving original equipment manufacturers and cloud service providers. For its most recent annual reporting period, two customers each accounted for 10% or more of net revenue, and the 10 largest customers collectively accounted for 82% of net revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached nearly $9.5 billion. This figure reflects growth of close to 30.6% over the previous 12 months as the company expanded its footprint in AI infrastructure. Net income for the same period was approximately $2.6 billion, marking a significant turnaround from previous years.

Story Continues

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.3. Its current ratio is approximately 2, indicating a solid ability to meet short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was close to $1.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 33.8% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Risk profile comparison

Applied Materials faces significant geographic concentration, with a heavy reliance on customers in China. This exposure makes the company sensitive to trade policies and export restrictions. It also manages legal risks involving export controls, including a $252 million settlement reached in February 2026 for export violations involving Semiconductor Manufacturing International. Furthermore, its reliance on complex global supply chains creates vulnerability to regional disruptions or inventory obsolescence.

Marvell Technology has high customer concentration. Its 10 largest clients account for nearly 82% of revenue, and it often competes with rivals like Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO). The company is also navigating a massive $115 billion pending acquisition of Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE). This deal introduces risks related to shareholder dilution and the complex process of integrating two large organizations. Additionally, Marvell's dependency on third-party foundries in the Pacific Rim creates supply chain risks if regional political conflicts arise.

Applied Materials currently appears to be the more conservative value choice, while Marvell Technology commands a higher premium given its faster growth profile.

Which stock would I buy for 2027?

Marvell and Applied Materials are riding the current tech boom, with both stocks hitting all-time highs earlier this year. They've since pulled back a considerable amount, but they're still handily outpacing the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) by massive margins:

There's the possibility of dilution, but there's also the potential that the combined company doesn't create the cost-savings and synergies management had hoped for. That could lead to significant writedowns, which would almost certainly impact the stock negatively.

Applied Materials just seems to have less risk, which makes it my pick for 2027 and beyond.

news.Content:
Have you evaluated the performance of Cirrus Logic's (CRUS) international operations during the quarter that concluded in September 2026? Considering the extensive worldwide presence of this chipmaker, analyzing the patterns in international revenues is crucial for understanding its financial resilience and potential for growth.

In the current era of a tightly interconnected global economy, the proficiency of a company to penetrate international markets significantly influences its financial health and trajectory of growth. For investors, the key is to grasp how reliant a company is on overseas markets, as this provides insights into the durability of its earnings, its ability to exploit different economic cycles, and its overall growth capabilities.

Presence in international markets can act as a hedge against domestic economic downturns and provide access to faster-growing economies. However, this diversification also brings complexities due to currency fluctuations, geopolitical risks and differing market dynamics.
